units.text: INT. WOMAN - CONTINUOUS
Gerald cannot separate his future from my past.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: That is exactly what he should do. That is exactly what you should help him to do. What a typical woman you are! You talk sentimentally, and you are thoroughly selfish the whole time. But don’t let us have a scene. Rachel, I want you to look at this matter from the common-sense point of view, from the point of view of what is best for our son, leaving you and me out of the question. What is our son at present? An underpaid clerk in a small Provincial Bank in a third-rate English town. If you imagine he is quite happy in such a position, you are mistaken. He is thoroughly discontented.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: He was not discontented till he met you. You have made him so.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: Of course, I made him so. Discontent is the first step in the progress of a man or a nation. But I did not leave him with a mere longing for things he could not get. No, I made him a charming offer. He jumped at it, I need hardly say. Any young man would. And now, simply because it turns out that I am the boy’s own father and he my own son, you propose practically to ruin his career. That is to say, if I were a perfect stranger, you would allow Gerald to go away with me, but as he is my own flesh and blood you won’t. How utterly illogical you are!
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: I will not allow him to go.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: How can you prevent it? What excuse can you give to him for making him decline such an offer as mine? I won’t tell him in what relations I stand to him, I need hardly say. But you daren’t tell him. You know that. Look how you have brought him up.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: I have brought him up to be a good man.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: Quite so. And what is the result? You have educated him to be your judge if he ever finds you out. And a bitter, an unjust judge he will be to you. Don’t be deceived, Rachel. Children begin by loving their parents. After a time they judge them. Rarely, if ever, do they forgive them.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: George, don’t take my son away from me. I have had twenty years of sorrow, and I have only had one thing to love me, only one thing to love. You have had a life of joy, and pleasure, and success. You have been quite happy, you have never thought of us. There was no reason, according to your views of life, why you should have remembered us at all. Your meeting us was a mere accident, a horrible accident. Forget it. Don’t come now, and rob me of . . . of all I have in the whole world. You are so rich in other things. Leave me the little vineyard of my life; leave me the walled-in garden and the well of water; the ewe-lamb God sent me, in pity or in wrath, oh! leave me that. George, don’t take Gerald from me.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: Rachel, at the present moment you are not necessary to Gerald’s career; I am. There is nothing more to be said on the subject.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: I will not let him go.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: Here is Gerald. He has a right to decide for himself.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: Enter GERALD.
Well, dear mother, I hope you have settled it all with Lord Illingworth?
units.name: GERALD

units.text: I have not, Gerald.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: Your mother seems not to like your coming with me, for some reason.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: Why, mother?
units.name: GERALD

units.text: I thought you were quite happy here with me, Gerald. I didn’t know you were so anxious to leave me.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: Mother, how can you talk like that? Of course I have been quite happy with you. But a man can’t stay always with his mother. No chap does. I want to make myself a position, to do something. I thought you would have been proud to see me Lord Illingworth’s secretary.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: I do not think you would be suitable as a private secretary to Lord Illingworth. You have no qualifications.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: I don’t wish to seem to interfere for a moment, Mrs. Arbuthnot, but as far as your last objection is concerned, I surely am the best judge. And I can only tell you that your son has all the qualifications I had hoped for. He has more, in fact, than I had even thought of. Far more.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: MRS. ARBUTHNOT remains silent .
Have you any other reason, Mrs. Arbuthnot, why you don’t wish your son to accept this post?
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: Have you, mother? Do answer.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: If you have, Mrs. Arbuthnot, pray, pray say it. We are quite by ourselves here. Whatever it is, I need not say I will not repeat it.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: Mother?
units.name: GERALD

units.text: If you would like to be alone with your son, I will leave you. You may have some other reason you don’t wish me to hear.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: I have no other reason.
units.name: MRS. ARBUTHNOT

units.text: Then, my dear boy, we may look on the thing as settled. Come, you and I will smoke a cigarette on the terrace together. And Mrs. Arbuthnot, pray let me tell you, that I think you have acted very, very wisely.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: Exit with GERALD.
MRS. ARBUTHNOT is left alone .
She stands immobile with a look of unutterable sorrow on her face .
The Picture Gallery at Hunstanton .
Door at back leading on to terrace .
LORD ILLINGWORTH and GERALD, R.C. LORD ILLINGWORTH lolling on a sofa .
GERALD in a chair .
Thoroughly sensible woman, your mother, Gerald. I knew she would come round in the end.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: My mother is awfully conscientious, Lord Illingworth, and I know she doesn’t think I am educated enough to be your secretary. She is perfectly right, too. I was fearfully idle when I was at school, and I couldn’t pass an examination now to save my life.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: My dear Gerald, examinations are of no value whatsoever. If a man is a gentleman, he knows quite enough, and if he is not a gentleman, whatever he knows is bad for him.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: But I am so ignorant of the world, Lord Illingworth.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: Don’t be afraid, Gerald. Remember that you’ve got on your side the most wonderful thing in the world—youth! There is nothing like youth. The middle-aged are mortgaged to Life. The old are in life’s lumber-room. But youth is the Lord of Life. Youth has a kingdom waiting for it. Every one is born a king, and most people die in exile, like most kings. To win back my youth, Gerald, there is nothing I wouldn’t do—except take exercise, get up early, or be a useful member of the community.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: But you don’t call yourself old, Lord Illingworth?
units.name: GERALD

units.text: I am old enough to be your father, Gerald.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: I don’t remember my father; he died years ago.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: So Lady Hunstanton told me.
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: It is very curious, my mother never talks to me about my father. I sometimes think she must have married beneath her.
units.name: GERALD

units.text: Winces slightly .
Really?
units.name: LORD ILLINGWORTH

units.text: Goes over and puts his hand on GERALD’S shoulder .
